claim: isAccessTokenId() compares the wrong substring (chars 3-5, not 4-6) and returns false on a MATCH, so it never checks the grant shortcut and the new event assertions verify nothing about grant type.
The fourth requireNonNull checks grantType again instead of rawTokenId, so a null rawTokenId is accepted and encodes as the literal 'null' in the jti.
body:
## [ISSUE] Null check for `rawTokenId` tests `grantType` again

**Severity:** LOW — the constructor's null-check contract has a copy-paste mistake. A null raw ID is accepted silently and shows up later as `...:null`.

### The Problem
```java
Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null grantType not allowed");
Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");   // line 73
```
Line 73 checks `grantType` a second time, and `rawTokenId` is never checked.

### Theory / Proof
`DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId` builds `... + ':' + tokenContext.getRawTokenId()`. Java string concatenation turns `null` into `"null"`, so a context built with a null raw ID produces a jti like `onrtac:null`. That is not unique across tokens, and it breaks revocation keyed by jti. `TokenContextEncoderProvider` is a public SPI, so custom providers and callers can build `AccessTokenContext` directly. The constructor is where this should be caught.

### What happens today vs. what will break
The only production caller today passes `KeycloakModelUtils.generateId()`, which is never null. Any future caller, or a custom `TokenContextEncoderProvider` that passes a null raw ID (for example from a parsed token without `jti`), would get a colliding `...:null` ID with no error, even though the message says null is not allowed.

### Research
`java.util.Objects.requireNonNull(T obj, String message)` only validates its first argument.

### Recommendation
```java
Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");
```

claim: Only grants going through createTokenResponse (plus password, refresh, pre-authorized code and standard token exchange) set Constants.GRANT_TYPE; client_credentials, UMA (pg), implicit/hybrid and legacy V1 token exchange tokens are all encoded with grant 'na'.
body:
## [GAP ANALYSIS] `client_credentials`, UMA, implicit and V1 token-exchange access tokens are encoded with grant `na`

**Severity:** MEDIUM — the grant type in the jti is missing for one of the most common grants (`client_credentials`) and for several others. Consumers planned in #37117 / #37662 cannot rely on it.

### The Problem
The PR sets the grant type on the `ClientSessionContext` in a few specific places:
- `OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse` (line 109): authorization_code, CIBA, device
- `ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType` line 134
- `TokenManager.refreshAccessToken` line 248
- `PreAuthorizedCodeGrantType` line 82
- `StandardTokenExchangeProvider` line 237

Other token-issuing paths call `responseBuilder(...).generateAccessToken()` directly and never set `Constants.GRANT_TYPE`:
- `ClientCredentialsGrantType.process()` (line 141: `tokenManager.responseBuilder(...).generateAccessToken()`)
- `AuthorizationTokenService` line ~358 (UMA ticket / `PermissionGrantType`, whose factory adds shortcut `pg`)
- `OIDCLoginProtocol` line ~272 (implicit/hybrid `response_type=token`)
- `AbstractTokenExchangeProvider` line ~410 (legacy V1 token exchange)

For all of these, `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` finds no attribute and falls back to `UNKNOWN` (`"na"`).

### Theory / Proof
The `pg` shortcut added in `PermissionGrantTypeFactory` can never appear in a token, because no code path sets `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:uma-ticket` on the context. Token exchange also gets different encodings depending on the provider: V2 tokens get `te`, V1 tokens get `na`. The PR description gives token exchange (#37117) as a motivating use case.

### What happens today vs. what will break
Nothing reads the encoding yet, so nothing is broken right now. Once #37117 / #37662 start branching on `AccessTokenContext.getGrantType()`, a service-account token (`trrtna:...` or `onrtna:...`) cannot be told apart from any other unclassified token, and UMA RPTs never report `uma-ticket`.

### Research
Every place that mints an access token needs to set the context. The PR already does this for password grant by setting the attribute right after `processor.attachSession()`. The same one-line pattern works for the other paths.

### Recommendation
Set the attribute in the missing paths, for example in `ClientCredentialsGrantType`:
```java
ClientSessionContext clientSessionCtx = TokenManager.attachAuthenticationSession(session, userSession, authSession);
clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, context.getGrantType());
```
Do the same in `AuthorizationTokenService` (`OAuth2Constants.UMA_GRANT_TYPE`), `AbstractTokenExchangeProvider` (`OAuth2Constants.TOKEN_EXCHANGE_GRANT_TYPE`) and implicit flow. A more robust option is to set it once in `TokenEndpoint` before dispatching to the grant, so new grants cannot forget it. Add `expectClientCredentials`-style assertions with `isAccessTokenId("cc")`.

claim: Adding an abstract getShortcut() to OAuth2GrantTypeFactory makes existing custom grant-type factories fail: compiled jars throw AbstractMethodError in DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit, which aborts server startup.

Shortcut length is never validated, and the OAuth2GrantTypeFactory Javadoc says 'usually like 3-letters'; a 3-char shortcut encodes fine but every resulting jti is rejected by getTokenContextFromTokenId (length != 6).
body:
## [ISSUE] Grant shortcut length contract (2 chars) is not documented or enforced; the Javadoc says 3 letters

**Severity:** MEDIUM — a custom grant that follows the Javadoc produces tokens whose IDs the same provider cannot decode.

### The Problem
`OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` Javadoc:
> @return usually like 3-letters shortcut of specific grants ...

The decoder in `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId` hard-codes a fixed layout:
```java
if (encodedContext.length() != 6) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("Incorrect token id: '" + encodedTokenId + "'. Expected length of 6.");
}
String gtShortcut = encodedContext.substring(4, 6);
```
`postInit` here (line 74) and `getShortcutByGrantType` accept any shortcut without checking its length. `encodeTokenId` also concatenates it unchecked.

### Theory / Proof
Take a custom grant with `getShortcut() == "jwt"`:
- `encodeTokenId` -> `onrtjwt:<uuid>` (prefix length 7). This succeeds and ships in the token.
- `getTokenContextFromTokenId("onrtjwt:<uuid>")` -> `IllegalArgumentException("Expected length of 6")`.

A 1-char shortcut fails the same way, and a shortcut containing `:` would move the separator. The encoding does not round-trip, and nothing reports the problem at startup.

### What happens today vs. what will break
All built-in shortcuts are 2 chars, so the built-in grants round-trip. The first custom grant written from the Javadoc's "3-letters" guidance, or any second consumer that calls `getTokenContextFromTokenId` (introspection / userinfo per #37662), gets `IllegalArgumentException` on every such token.

### Research
The PR description says the compact format relies on "every type has always 2 characters long shortcut". That invariant only exists in the author's head and in `substring` offsets, not in the SPI contract.

### Recommendation
Fix the Javadoc and validate once at startup:
```java
/**
 * @return exactly 2-character shortcut, unique across grants, used when encoding the grant into the access token ID
 */
String getShortcut();
```
```java
String grantShortcut = gtf.getShortcut();
if (grantShortcut == null || grantShortcut.length() != 2 || grantShortcut.indexOf(':') != -1) {
    throw new IllegalStateException("Grant type '" + grantName + "' must provide a 2-character shortcut, but was: '" + grantShortcut + "'");
}
```
Apply the same check in the lazy-refresh path of `getShortcutByGrantType`.

claim: The lazy refresh in getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut skips the duplicate-shortcut validation done in postInit, so a later-registered grant with a colliding shortcut silently overwrites the reverse mapping and makes earlier tokens decode to the wrong grant.

testIncorrectGrantType passes only because sessionFactory is null and getGrantTypeByShortcut throws NullPointerException; it catches RuntimeException so it never verifies the intended IllegalArgumentException.
body:
## [ISSUE] `testIncorrectGrantType` passes on a `NullPointerException`, not the intended validation error

**Severity:** LOW — the test does not cover the "unknown grant shortcut" branch it is named after.

### The Problem
The test sets up the factory with only `init(null)` and hand-filled maps. `postInit` is never called, so `sessionFactory` is `null`. For `"ofrtac:5678"`, `ac` is not in `grantsByShortcuts`, so `getGrantTypeByShortcut` goes to the refresh branch:
```java
sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(OAuth2GrantType.class)  // sessionFactory == null -> NPE
```
The test catches `RuntimeException`, so the NPE counts as a pass:
```java
} catch (RuntimeException iae) {
    // ignored
}
```

### Theory / Proof
The `IllegalArgumentException("... Unknown value 'ac' for grant type")` branch in `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId` never runs in this test. If that branch were deleted or broken, the test would still pass.

### What happens today vs. what will break
The test is green but proves nothing about the error path. A future change that returns `UNKNOWN` instead of throwing, or that breaks the refresh lookup, would not be caught.

### Research
JUnit 4.13 `Assert.assertThrows(Class, ThrowingRunnable)` checks the exact exception type.

### Recommendation
Give the factory a stub session factory, or skip the refresh when it is null, and assert the specific exception:
```java
IllegalArgumentException e = Assert.assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
        () -> provider.getTokenContextFromTokenId("ofrtac:5678"));
Assert.assertTrue(e.getMessage().contains("grant type"));
```
